implementation_notes: Python subclasses share both the declared type and its implementation through ordinary (multiple) inheritance, and abc.ABC plus @abstractmethod make the layer base non-instantiable until every abstract member is implemented, so the contract is enforced rather than documented. Mixins - small, usually state-free base classes - are the idiomatic way to add one slice of the layer's shared behavior, and cooperative super() calls keep the whole chain working instead of hard-wiring the direct parent. The classic base-first form stays right when the layer owns identity and state (ids, version counters, audit fields); when the shared behavior is a single concern, prefer an independent mixin composed into each class.
code_sketch:
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class LayerObject(ABC):              # the declared type of the layer
    def __init__(self, id: int) -> None:
        self.id, self.version = id, 0
    def touch(self) -> None:         # shared implementation
        self.version += 1
    @abstractmethod
    def describe(self) -> str: ...   # required of every layer member

class User(LayerObject):             # inherits id/version/touch, supplies describe
    def describe(self) -> str: return f"user {self.id}"
pitfalls: Abstract methods only block instantiation while ABCMeta is in the metaclass chain; a subclass that implements nothing but is never instantiated silently keeps the hole.
Mixins participate in the MRO and in cooperative initialization: a mixin whose __init__ does not call super().__init__() breaks the chain for every class below it.
Multiple inheritance makes the layer more than one type, and name collisions resolve by MRO order, which is invisible at the call site.

variants.name: ORM declarative base (Django abstract model / SQLAlchemy DeclarativeBase)
variants.implementation_notes: When the layer is already ORM-mapped the framework supplies the layer supertype: a Django model with class Meta: abstract = True contributes its fields to every subclass without creating a table, and SQLAlchemy's DeclarativeBase or a mixin adds columns, mapper options and table naming to every mapped class. The shared state (id, timestamps, version) then doubles as mapping configuration, and the mapper treats every member uniformly. Choose this route when persistence defines the layer; keep the plain abc base when the layer must stay persistence-ignorant.
variants.code_sketch:
class BaseModel(models.Model):                  # the layer supertype, no table
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    class Meta:
        abstract = True

class User(BaseModel):                          # fields copied to its own table
    email = models.EmailField()
pitfalls: Django sets abstract = False for children, so an abstract base does not stay abstract through a second level unless every intermediate class repeats it.
SQLAlchemy copies a mixin's columns into each mapped class; relationships and table arguments must use declared_attr or declared_attr.directive to be evaluated per subclass.
Framework base metadata leaks into the layer: adding a field to the base changes every subclass schema at once.
